saved in the card's header. Before changing an assignment it flushes pending
writes to the card. The changed drive's directory is read afresh on its

so that access uses the new volume.

A card changed on a PC needs a reset when returned to the board. Warm boot
retains cached card blocks and the drives' free-space state, so it does not
reinitialise the card or discard those old copies. Only cold boot starts
the card again. Do not let TEC-OS and a PC write the same card at the same time.

including ATOM, but does not itself produce the ROM or media.
[Chapter 26](26-build-the-rom-and-media.md) gives the source/input preparation
and build route through `npm run media`, which writes the ROM, starter image,
recipes and component files into `dist/`. A host-assembled COM program reaches

`get` copies a named file to the PC. Its optional output-file argument gives
the destination. A named destination is overwritten if it already exists, so
use a new path for a recovered copy. Without that argument the bytes go to
standard output. Binary extraction includes every recorded 128-byte record,
including padding in the last one. With `--text`, extraction stops before the
first `^Z` and converts carriage-return/line-feed pairs to line feeds. A lone
carriage return is retained. Without `^Z`, all recorded bytes undergo that
conversion, including any padding.

The card holds programs, resident services, `STARTUP.CMD` and your files.
Each drive uses a volume, an ordinary CP/M disk of a fixed size. CP/M 2.2
addresses at most 8 MiB on a drive. Most CP/M machines used floppy disks
of a few hundred KiB, while an SD card can hold many volumes.

occurrences.full_context:
The container occupies 20,480 blocks or 10 MiB. SYSTEM begins at block
2,048, 1 MiB into the card, and occupies 1 MiB. WORK starts at block 4,096
and occupies 8 MiB. The default alignment puts each volume on a multiple of
2,048 blocks, a common SD erase-block multiple. On this two-volume image
the space before SYSTEM contains only the header and unused padding.

CP/M reads and writes 128-byte records. Four records fit a 512-byte card
block. Space is allocated to files in larger allocation blocks, so a file
with any data occupies at least 2 KiB on G1M or 4 KiB on G8M. The one-record
`STARTUP.CMD` therefore occupies 4 KiB on WORK even though its recorded
length is only 128 bytes.

occurrences.full_context:
Registers hold the values passed to a call. `A`, `B`, `C` and `E` each
hold a byte. `BC`, `DE` and `HL` are 16-bit register pairs, large enough
for a memory address. To select a BDOS operation, you put its function number in `C` and
call `0005h`. A byte parameter goes in `E`, while an address or word
parameter goes in `DE`. A byte result is returned in `A` and a word result
in `HL`. For example, function 2 takes the character in `E` and function 9
takes an address in `DE`. In source, `BDOS EQU $0005` gives that call
address a name.

`0000h` on the inherited stack before jumping to `0100h`. A top-level `RET`
therefore ends the program through the warm-boot jump at `0000h`. Calls
within the program must return before that last `RET`, so it reaches the
word supplied by the CCP.

It is a 36-byte block through

occurrences.full_context:
The sequential position is split between an *extent*, a group of 128
records, and the record within it. `EX` and `S2` identify the extent.
`CR` selects its next record, normally 0 to 127. At the boundary the BDOS
moves to the next extent as needed. You keep the complete FCB between
calls so those updates and its allocation map remain available.
Appendix A gives the full field contracts and random-record operations.

occurrences.full_context:
The FCB holds file state, while the bytes being read or written go through
a separate memory buffer. The BDOS calls this the *DMA address*. It is a
transfer address in your memory, not a request to program a hardware DMA
controller. Initially it is `0080h`, with room for one 128-byte record.
Function 26 changes it to the address supplied in `DE`.

occurrences.full_context:
SHOW only reads, so it leaves no changed file state to close. A program that
writes must close its updated FCB before finishing. Warm boot flushes pending
writes from the block cache but cannot close the program's FCBs. The write
sequence after SHOW explains how to finish both operations and check them.

Writing uses an FCB and a DMA buffer in the same way, but the state
must reach the directory before the program finishes. For a new file,
prepare all 36 FCB bytes: the drive, the space-padded name/type and zeroed
state. Choose a name that is not already present. Function 22, make file,
creates a directory entry. It is not a replace-file command.

Page zero occupies `0000h–00FFh` and contains the CP/M jumps and buffers. The
*transient program area*, or TPA, begins at `0100h`. Its upper bound is the
address stored in the jump at `0005h`, read as a word at `0006h`. That address
is the first byte outside the TPA. Your final usable byte is one below it.

A program checks the signature and major version before calling `C008h`. The
major must be exactly 5. A new major may renumber services, while a new minor
adds numbers at the end. Code using the 5.0 calls can therefore run on 5.1. A
program requiring an added minor-version call must check that version too.

occurrences.full_context:
The other numbers extend the same ABI. Numbers 9–11 mount, unmount and describe
volumes, as Chapter 17 explains. Number 12 registers the GLCD video-driver
table. Numbers 13 and 14 find or enumerate named records in the registry
described in Chapter 13. Those registry calls have their own result convention,
including a generation in A, so their callers test carry rather than applying

5.1.

The hardware services use the caller's stack. PUTAT has the largest bound: 22
bytes below the return address supplied by CALL. That fits the inherited 30-byte
allowance from Chapter 10, but a caller must also count its own nested calls and
saved registers. Appendix B lists the individual bounds. These are bounds, not
newly measured peaks.

A screen-layout program uses the size INFO returns. With a serial console, both

With B = 120, the interval is 1,971 T-states and the frequency is about 1,015
Hz. DE = 400 gives about 0.2 seconds, as in LCDMSG. For a duration in seconds,
the half-cycle count is frequency × 2 × seconds. B = 0 counts as 256, giving
about 482 Hz, while B = 1 gives about 29,851 Hz. DE = 0 returns immediately
without sound. These are instruction-derived relationships. Appendix B
distinguishes the final interval and call overhead.

during the sound. A nonempty tone ends with the speaker off. The routine keeps
the serial transmit line idle while driving the speaker.

A release restores the ROM PICO console's mode, font and displayed page when
that console started at cold boot. If it is the selected console, the release
also clears the screen and homes the cursor. With the Matrix switch disabled
the PICO console did not start, so release leaves the chip's programmed state

The claim records a flag rather than an owner identity. Warm boot releases it
through the same path, so an exiting program's claim ends too. Release with no
active claim does nothing and returns status 0.

On the 8-row graphics LCD, PLACE's row 10 is below the display, so it writes
nothing and reports status 0. On serial it reports status 2. It also reports 2
while the PICO is both claimed and the console. A claim on PICO leaves PUTAT
available on the graphics-LCD console. Portable code checks the ABI before PUTAT
and retains a BDOS path for status 2.

occurrences.full_context:
Either way, the record's 128 bytes are then copied from the DMA address into
the line with `CWRREC`, and `CDSET` marks the line dirty. On a volume
written behind a data write ends there. Success at this point means the
record is in the cache. A miss may already have forced an older dirty line
to the card, so the complete call need not leave the card unchanged. A write
of type 1, a directory write, which bit 0 of `CWTYPE` shows, goes on
(`src/cache.asm:596-613`, `src/cache.asm:632-651`). The new directory entry
must not reach the card before the data blocks it names. `CFLUSH` writes
every dirty line except the directory's, and then, if every one was written,
`CWRITE` writes the directory's line. The data reaches the card before the
directory block that names it. If any of those writes fails, the directory's
cached line is dropped, so its next read comes from the card. A data line
whose write fails stays dirty, since it holds the only copy of its records.
The write then reports the error to the BDOS. When function 45 returns the
error to a program, another close can retry the retained dirty data. If
those writes and the directory write succeed, the close succeeds
(`src/cache.asm:307-350`, `src/cache.asm:632-651`).

occurrences.full_context:
`CWRITE` writes a single line to the card (`src/cache.asm:247-290`). It
takes the block number from the table and sets `SDXB` so that `SDWRITE`
reads its 512 bytes straight from the line in EXPAND 1. On success it marks
the line clean. On a failure it leaves the line dirty and returns `NZ`. A
flush writes every dirty line, goes on past each failure and returns `NZ` if
there was one. `CFLALL` drops each line whose write fails, so the card's
copy of that block stands. `CFLUSH`, the directory write's, leaves such a
line dirty for a later flush (`src/cache.asm:307-350`). `CTAKE`'s write of
one line, when every line is dirty, keeps a failed line dirty in the same
way. `CTAKE` then returns the error with `CNEXT` moved past the line. The
next miss writes the line after it, so a single bad block can't fail every
later miss (`src/cache.asm:402-423`).

occurrences.full_context:
A `^C` at the prompt causes a warm boot. When its flush succeeds, every
pending cache change has reached the card. A failure prints `Write lost`,
whose consequence is described below. Reset does not flush the old cache. Cold boot clears EXPAND 1
(`src/boot.asm:321-346`), so changes still unwritten at reset are lost. Some changes since the last
directory write may already be on the card. `CTAKE` wrote them when their
lines were given out for other blocks (`src/cache.asm:402-409`). The card
can then hold a mix of old and new blocks.

occurrences.full_context:
A data write on a volume written behind can return success before its record
has reached the card. A failure when its line goes to the card later
therefore needs a report of its own, and that report is `Write lost`.
`CWBOOT` calls `CFLALL` at the warm boot. That writes every dirty line and
drops each one the card rejects. If any failed, `CWBOOT` drops the rest of a
chained line and prints `Write lost` on its own line
(`src/cache.asm:661-668`, `src/text.asm:93`). The dropped lines' changes are
gone from RAM. Blocks the card rejected before programming retain their
earlier contents. A partially programmed block has the corruption risk
described above. The message is printed once for that flush. With no new
dirty data, the next warm boot has nothing more to write.

occurrences.full_context:
A directory write whose flush fails during a program's run is the BDOS's
`Bad Sector` instead. Its data lines that failed are still dirty, so the
warm boot after it writes them again. When the card rejects them again, the
boot prints `Write lost` and drops them. The directory's line was dropped
when the directory write failed. The failed directory update is not retried
by that flush. If the card rejected the directory write before changing it,
the previous directory remains. A card error or power loss during
programming can instead leave a partly changed block.

occurrences.full_context:
For a program that enables maskable interrupts, the protected portion of
a BIOS disk call holds them off across mapping, cache work and card I/O.
A read that misses holds them off for about 235,000 T-states, 59 milliseconds. A directory
write on the volume written behind holds them off while every dirty line is
written. In the retained `78127ec` run the close of a file of four blocks
took 1,111,542 T-states. The retained `78127ec` per-line `CWRITE` cost was
217,421 T-states. Multiplying it by 30 gives about 6.5 million T-states, or
1.6 seconds, for data transfer alone. That is an estimate from the model
cost, not a measured all-dirty flush or an upper bound for a physical card.
A program with an interrupt response requirement can place disk calls
outside the interval that needs a short response. Writing through avoids a
directory-triggered all-line flush on that volume, but a cache miss may
still write one dirty line. Warm boot, mount changes and function 48 can
flush the whole cache whatever volume the program uses. Those operations
must also fall outside that interval.

of the drive. The map holds 16 one-byte block numbers on a volume of 256

Make searches in mode 3 for the first empty entry. It fills
the entry with the FCB's name, the current user number and an empty map, and
writes the entry's directory record at once
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:558-643`). As in CP/M 2.2 it clears `S2` and keeps
`EX`, so the entry is the extent `EX` names among the file's first 32. It
clears `S1`, `RC` and the map in the FCB too
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:529-539`, `src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:574-591`). Make
leaves `CR` and the random-record bytes alone. For a sequential file the
program supplies `CR` = 0, as in Chapter 9. Make returns an entry slot from
0 to 3, or `FFh` if the directory is full. Every directory write goes to the
BIOS as write type 1 (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:100-136`). On a volume written
behind, a directory write flushes the other dirty cache lines first, as
Chapter 18 describes (`src/cache.asm:632-651`).

Function 21 writes the record at `CR` (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:22-103`). If the
map has no block for the record, `ALLOCBLK` takes the first free block of
the drive. The record then goes to the BIOS as write type 2, the first write
to a new block (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:49-72`). For that type the BIOS obtains
the card block's cache line without a pre-read and clears it before copying
the record (`src/bios.asm:368-418`, `src/cache.asm:529-554`). Any other
write of a record is type 0. `CR` moves on only after the BIOS has returned
success, so a write that fails leaves the FCB on the record it didn't write
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:79-103`).

occurrences.full_context:
To read or write a record the BDOS needs the record's place on the volume.
`FCBADDR` takes the extent's place within its entry, `EX` AND `EXM`, times
128, adds `CR` and shifts the sum right by `BSH`. The result is the index of
the record's block in the map (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:617-648`). `POSREC` then
turns the block and record into a record number on the volume: the block
shifted left by `BSH`, plus `CR` AND `BLM` (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:871-908`).
The BIOS takes a track and a sector, so `POSREC` divides that number by
`SPT`. The division is `DIV16`, 16 steps of shift and trial subtraction. The
quotient goes to the BIOS through `SETTRK` and the remainder through
`SECTRAN` and `SETSEC` (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:910-977`). The BIOS's `MAPREC`
turns track and sector back into a record number, as Chapter 17 describes.
From that it takes `BLKOFF`, the card block within the volume, and
`BLKSLOT`, the record's quarter of it (`src/bios.asm:124-163`).

occurrences.full_context:
For a worked arithmetic example, take record 37 of extent 0 of a file on
drive A, a G1M volume, whose third map cell holds block 300. `FCBADDR` gives
0 × 128 + 37 = 37, and 37 shifted right by 4 is 2, the third cell. `POSREC`
shifts 300 left by 4 to get 4,800 and adds 37 AND 15, which is 5. The record
is 4,805 of the volume, and 4,805 divided by 64 is track 75, sector 5.
`MAPREC` makes 75 × 64 + 5 = 4,805 again. `BLKOFF` is 4,805 divided by 4,
card block 1,201 of the volume, and `BLKSLOT` is the remainder, 1. The card
block is the volume's start block plus 1,201 (`src/bios.asm:181-215`).

The write after record 127 finds `CR` at 128. It closes the extent, then
opens the next extent or makes it (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:23-35`,
`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-158`). The write returns 2 when the drive has no
free block. It returns 1 when the next extent needs a directory entry and
the directory is full. The FCB then stays on its extent with `CR` at 128, so
a write after an entry is freed makes the extent it needs
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-175`). It returns 1 in the same way when the close
of the extent it leaves finds no entry for it
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-126`). That is the case after the file was deleted
under the open FCB.

occurrences.full_context:
Function 16, close, returns 0 when it writes nothing, or the entry's slot
from 0 to 3 when it updates the directory. It returns `FFh` when that update
finds no matching entry (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:250-268`). It returns at once
when bit 7 of `S2` is still set, with nothing written
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:270-278`). On a read-only drive it also returns
success with nothing written (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:289-298`). Otherwise it
searches in mode 4 for the entry again and copies the FCB's extent, record
count and map into it, or only the map when the FCB is on an earlier extent
than the entry records. It then writes the directory record back
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:289-339`). On a volume written behind the directory
write flushes every other dirty cache line before writing its own line. A
failed flush is still an error, and earlier writes are not undone. Chapter
18 describes the resulting persistence boundary (`src/cache.asm:596-651`).

finds no matching entry (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:250-268`). It returns at once
when bit 7 of `S2` is still set, with nothing written
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:270-278`). On a read-only drive it also returns
success with nothing written (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:289-298`). Otherwise it
searches in mode 4 for the entry again and copies the FCB's extent, record
count and map into it, or only the map when the FCB is on an earlier extent
than the entry records. It then writes the directory record back
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:289-339`). On a volume written behind the directory
write flushes every other dirty cache line before writing its own line. A
failed flush is still an error, and earlier writes are not undone. Chapter
18 describes the resulting persistence boundary (`src/cache.asm:596-651`).

into the FCB (`src/cpm/bdosfn.asm:621-685`). A `?` in the FCB's name becomes

`ALLOCBLK` scans the vector from block 0 for the first clear bit, sets it
and puts the block's number in the FCB's map
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:683-774`). A delete clears the bits of each block the
entry lists (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:641-722`). The directory's own blocks are
set from `AL0` and `AL1` when the vector is built
(`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:503-532`), and they are never given out. The vector
changes as soon as a block is taken, before the file is closed. A block a
program has written but not yet closed is therefore already in use for every
other file. `ALLOCBLK` also marks the FCB as changed
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:733-763`). A close after a failed write can
still write the entry that holds the allocated block. Close can itself fail, so the entry is not guaranteed to reach the card
after a data-write error.
If the program exits without closing, the later vector rebuild derives
allocation from the directory again.

A vector is built when a drive is logged in, the first time it is selected
after a disk reset (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:202-350`). `LOGIN` calls the BIOS's
`SELDSK` for the drive's DPH, and a drive with no volume gets 0, which is
the `Select` error (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:212-222`). It copies from the DPH
the addresses of the translation table, the directory buffer, the DPB and
the vector. A volume the card marks read-only then goes into the read-only
vector (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:254-264`). For a drive not in `LOGINV`,
`INITALV` clears the vector and sets the directory's bits, and the drive's
bit in `LOGINV` is set. The whole directory is then read a record at a time.
`PARENT` sets the bit of every block that each entry in use lists and moves
the mark past the entry (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:268-350`,
`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:540-633`). A block number past the end of the volume
has no bit, and `BITPTR` passes over it (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:734-742`). The
drive still logs in, and a delete of that file passes over the number too.
For a drive already in `LOGINV`, `LOGIN` reads nothing: `LOGFAST` takes the
drive's mark from its DPH (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:362-385`).

The BIOS's part is in its `WRITE`, which tests whether the card block being
written is one of the directory's. For such a block it sets the changed flag
and raises the mark to the end of that block's 16 entries
(`src/bios.asm:309-366`). It does that for every write, so a program's own
directory write through BIOS `WRITE` sets the flag and raises the mark as
well. `DUSAVE` writes the BDOS's mark only when it is higher than the one
there, so the higher of the two stands.

- If the changed flag is set, the drive is taken out of `LOGINV` and put in
  `WARMV`, the vector of drives to rebuild to their mark
  (`src/ram.asm:260-261`). At its next selection `LOGIN` builds the vector
  again, but reads the directory only up to the mark
  (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:297-319`). The mark covers every entry recorded as
  used, so the scan can omit the remaining empty entries.
- If the flag is clear, `ALVSUM` adds up the vector's bytes with `SUMDE`,
  the routine that also sums the container's table
  (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:446-454`, `src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:473-496`,
  `src/volutil.asm:120-136`). If the sum is what `LOGDONE` stored, the drive
  stays logged in with its vector as it is. A different sum indicates a
  change that neither an allocation nor a directory write recorded, such as
  a stray write by a program. That drive is taken out of `LOGINV` and
  scanned in full at its next selection. Equal sums are not a byte-for-byte
  comparison of the vector.

The BDOS keeps its working state in RAM, from `BDOSRAM` up to the exclusive end
`BDOSRME`. In the retained `78127ec` map this is `BE76h–BEFFh`
(`78127ec:src/ram.asm:142-216`). The offered source defines the same block by
labels (`src/ram.asm:231-312`). Its 54-byte stack is at the top of that block
(`src/layout.asm:152`). Warm boot clears the block, as a fresh load of the BDOS
from disk would leave it, and sets the DMA address to `0080h`
(`src/boot.asm:530-539`). Two of the BDOS's variables are outside the block
because a warm boot must not clear them. `LOGINV`, in the BIOS's part of the
resident workspace, has a bit for each drive whose allocation vector the BDOS
has built (`src/ram.asm:62-65`). `PRGCODE`, the return code of function 108, is
above the RAM BIOS table, where only cold boot clears it (`src/ram.asm:386-388`,
`src/boot.asm:73-79`). Per-drive pointers and scan state are in the drive's DPH,
the 16-byte disk parameter header described in Chapter 17.

Each goes to `BDERR` with its message and code. What `BDERR` does is set by
the error mode, which function 45 puts in `ERRMODE`
(`src/cpm/bdos.asm:271-275`, `src/cpm/bdoscon.asm:47-72`). In the default
mode `DISKMSG` prints the message and `BDERR` waits for a key with `GETCHAR`
(`src/cpm/bdoscon.asm:108-137`). An ordinary key retained during message

resume key, with `^C` at that pause aborting
(`src/cpm/bdoscon.asm:318-350`). `CHDROP` then ends the program by warm boot, whatever the key, so the
function never returns to the program (`src/cpm/bdos.asm:115-119`). `CHDROP`
also drops the rest of a chained line, which Chapter 21 describes.

and the error's code in `H`. Nothing is printed and the rest of a chained

new line. Built-ins can move `CMDSTRT` to an argument. CON moves it again
for a separated width, so its error may name that width. `ERRGO` sets

zero set at piece entry. They finish at `MAINLOOP` or at `STARTED`, which

Both DIR and TYPE print through the pager. `PGINIT` takes `VHGT` and `VWID`,
or 24 rows and 80 columns for serial and reserves a row for `[more]`.
`PGPUT` resets its column at carriage return, steps back at backspace and
advances to the next multiple of eight at a tab. It counts
a new line at LF or before a printable character beyond the last column
(`src/cpm/ccpfile.asm:334-470`). At a pause function 6 reads a key without
echo. `UNMORE` erases the prompt with CR, six spaces and CR (`src/text.asm:32-33`).
The key mask
makes `#` equivalent to `^C` and `;` equivalent to Esc. `^C` and `#` drop
the chain. Esc, `Q`, `q` and `;` stop only the listing. Other keys continue
(`src/cpm/ccpfile.asm:475-520`). Chapter 21 explains the chain distinction.

through the pager until `1Ah`, the first Ctrl-Z, or the file's end. It then

SAVE erases an existing file, makes it again and writes two 128-byte records
per page from `0100h`. A failed make, write or close gives `NO SPACE`.

successful close records the partial file. The error path discards the
close result, so the message does not certify that update. Digital Research's
CP/M 2.2 SAVE leaves the file open on that path
(`src/cpm/ccpcmd.asm:356-445`).

heading_path.text: Appendix G. The TEC-1G as TEC-OS uses it
The hex keypad and its NMI

occurrences.full_context:
With the keypad NMI jumper fitted, a press raises a non-maskable interrupt. The
CPU pushes its return address and enters `0066h`, inside the default file
control block (FCB) at `005Ch–007Fh`. TEC-OS installs no NMI handler there. The
bytes can be file metadata rather than instructions, so a press can crash the
machine. The supported TEC-OS setup leaves the jumper off. The diagnostics ROM
has its own NMI test and different keypad instructions, which must not be
applied to an ordinary TEC-OS session.

occurrences.full_context:
A service file contains the bytes to install, the records it needs and the
positions that require relocation. Its on-disk header describes that work.
The loader overwrites some fields after using them, so an installed header
must be read differently from the file header below.

installation and gives the resident header. This reference retains a
historical GLCD.SVC dump to show the file fields and gap encoding together.

occurrences.full_context:
Registers hold the values passed to a call. `A`, `B`, `C` and `E` each
hold a byte. `BC`, `DE` and `HL` are 16-bit register pairs, large enough
for a memory address. To select a BDOS operation, you put its function number in `C` and
call `0005h`. A byte parameter goes in `E`, while an address or word
parameter goes in `DE`. A byte result is returned in `A` and a word result
in `HL`. For example, function 2 takes the character in `E` and function 9
takes an address in `DE`. In source, `BDOS EQU $0005` gives that call
address a name.

`0000h` on the inherited stack before jumping to `0100h`. A top-level `RET`
therefore ends the program through the warm-boot jump at `0000h`. Calls
within the program must return before that last `RET`, so it reaches the
word supplied by the CCP.

the first argument as a *file control block*, or FCB, at `005Ch`.
It is a 36-byte block through
which the BDOS identifies a file and maintains the state of its operations.

occurrences.full_context:
The sequential position is split between an *extent*, a group of 128
records, and the record within it. `EX` and `S2` identify the extent.
`CR` selects its next record, normally 0 to 127. At the boundary the BDOS
moves to the next extent as needed. You keep the complete FCB between
calls so those updates and its allocation map remain available.
Appendix A gives the full field contracts and random-record operations.
manual_classification_hints: inline code retained in context, excluded from matching

occurrences.full_context:
The FCB holds file state, while the bytes being read or written go through
a separate memory buffer. The BDOS calls this the *DMA address*. It is a
transfer address in your memory, not a request to program a hardware DMA
controller. Initially it is `0080h`, with room for one 128-byte record.
Function 26 changes it to the address supplied in `DE`.
manual_classification_hints: inline code retained in context, excluded from matching

occurrences.full_context:
SHOW only reads, so it leaves no changed file state to close. A program that
writes must close its updated FCB before finishing. Warm boot flushes pending
writes from the block cache but cannot close the program's FCBs. The write
sequence after SHOW explains how to finish both operations and check them.

Writing uses an FCB and a DMA buffer in the same way, but the state
must reach the directory before the program finishes. For a new file,
prepare all 36 FCB bytes: the drive, the space-padded name/type and zeroed
state. Choose a name that is not already present. Function 22, make file,
creates a directory entry. It is not a replace-file command.

Page zero occupies `0000h–00FFh` and contains the CP/M jumps and buffers. The

`CTAKE` gives out lines in turn (`src/cache.asm:364-423`). A clean line can
be given out at any time, since the card has the same bytes. A dirty line
has to reach the card first. So `CTAKE` starts at `CNEXT` and gives out the
first clean line from there on. It passes over dirty ones and wraps from
line 29 to line 0. It sets `CNEXT` to the line after the one it gave out.
When every line is dirty, `CTAKE` writes the line at `CNEXT` to the card
first and gives out that one. The order is round-robin and not least
recently used. A block that is read often is still given up when its turn
comes, and read again from the card at its next use.

A data write on a volume written behind can return success before its record
has reached the card. A failure when its line goes to the card later
therefore needs a report of its own, and that report is `Write lost`.
`CWBOOT` calls `CFLALL` at the warm boot. That writes every dirty line and
drops each one the card rejects. If any failed, `CWBOOT` drops the rest of a
chained line and prints `Write lost` on its own line
(`src/cache.asm:661-668`, `src/text.asm:93`). The dropped lines' changes are
gone from RAM. Blocks the card rejected before programming retain their
earlier contents. A partially programmed block has the corruption risk
described above. The message is printed once for that flush. With no new
dirty data, the next warm boot has nothing more to write.

must also fall outside that interval.

A CP/M file is a sequence of 128-byte records. The BDOS finds them through
the directory, a table of 32-byte entries at the start of the volume. Each
entry names a file in a user area and holds a map of allocation block
numbers, the blocks of the volume that hold the file's records. In this

bytes of the card, as in Chapter 17. A program names a file in an FCB of 36

and map as the program reads and writes (`src/cpm/bdosfn.asm:621-685`,
`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:184-207`, `src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:227-298`). The attribute
bits are tested at byte 9 for read-only and byte 10 for system

of the drive. The map holds 16 one-byte block numbers on a volume of 256
blocks or fewer and 8 two-byte numbers otherwise. `FCBLOCK` and `BLOCKIDX`

Make searches in mode 3 for the first empty entry. It fills
the entry with the FCB's name, the current user number and an empty map, and
writes the entry's directory record at once
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:558-643`). As in CP/M 2.2 it clears `S2` and keeps
`EX`, so the entry is the extent `EX` names among the file's first 32. It
clears `S1`, `RC` and the map in the FCB too
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:529-539`, `src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:574-591`). Make
leaves `CR` and the random-record bytes alone. For a sequential file the
program supplies `CR` = 0, as in Chapter 9. Make returns an entry slot from
0 to 3, or `FFh` if the directory is full. Every directory write goes to the
BIOS as write type 1 (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:100-136`). On a volume written
behind, a directory write flushes the other dirty cache lines first, as
Chapter 18 describes (`src/cache.asm:632-651`).

Function 21 writes the record at `CR` (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:22-103`). If the
map has no block for the record, `ALLOCBLK` takes the first free block of
the drive. The record then goes to the BIOS as write type 2, the first write
to a new block (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:49-72`). For that type the BIOS obtains
the card block's cache line without a pre-read and clears it before copying
the record (`src/bios.asm:368-418`, `src/cache.asm:529-554`). Any other
write of a record is type 0. `CR` moves on only after the BIOS has returned
success, so a write that fails leaves the FCB on the record it didn't write
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:79-103`).

occurrences.full_context:
To read or write a record the BDOS needs the record's place on the volume.
`FCBADDR` takes the extent's place within its entry, `EX` AND `EXM`, times
128, adds `CR` and shifts the sum right by `BSH`. The result is the index of
the record's block in the map (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:617-648`). `POSREC` then
turns the block and record into a record number on the volume: the block
shifted left by `BSH`, plus `CR` AND `BLM` (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:871-908`).
The BIOS takes a track and a sector, so `POSREC` divides that number by
`SPT`. The division is `DIV16`, 16 steps of shift and trial subtraction. The
quotient goes to the BIOS through `SETTRK` and the remainder through
`SECTRAN` and `SETSEC` (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:910-977`). The BIOS's `MAPREC`
turns track and sector back into a record number, as Chapter 17 describes.
From that it takes `BLKOFF`, the card block within the volume, and
`BLKSLOT`, the record's quarter of it (`src/bios.asm:124-163`).

occurrences.full_context:
For a worked arithmetic example, take record 37 of extent 0 of a file on
drive A, a G1M volume, whose third map cell holds block 300. `FCBADDR` gives
0 × 128 + 37 = 37, and 37 shifted right by 4 is 2, the third cell. `POSREC`
shifts 300 left by 4 to get 4,800 and adds 37 AND 15, which is 5. The record
is 4,805 of the volume, and 4,805 divided by 64 is track 75, sector 5.
`MAPREC` makes 75 × 64 + 5 = 4,805 again. `BLKOFF` is 4,805 divided by 4,
card block 1,201 of the volume, and `BLKSLOT` is the remainder, 1. The card
block is the volume's start block plus 1,201 (`src/bios.asm:181-215`).

The write after record 127 finds `CR` at 128. It closes the extent, then
opens the next extent or makes it (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:23-35`,
`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-158`). The write returns 2 when the drive has no
free block. It returns 1 when the next extent needs a directory entry and
the directory is full. The FCB then stays on its extent with `CR` at 128, so
a write after an entry is freed makes the extent it needs
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-175`). It returns 1 in the same way when the close
of the extent it leaves finds no entry for it
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-126`). That is the case after the file was deleted
under the open FCB.

Function 16, close, returns 0 when it writes nothing, or the entry's slot
from 0 to 3 when it updates the directory. It returns `FFh` when that update
finds no matching entry (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:250-268`). It returns at once
when bit 7 of `S2` is still set, with nothing written
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:270-278`). On a read-only drive it also returns
success with nothing written (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:289-298`). Otherwise it
searches in mode 4 for the entry again and copies the FCB's extent, record
count and map into it, or only the map when the FCB is on an earlier extent
than the entry records. It then writes the directory record back
(`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:289-339`). On a volume written behind the directory
write flushes every other dirty cache line before writing its own line. A
failed flush is still an error, and earlier writes are not undone. Chapter
18 describes the resulting persistence boundary (`src/cache.asm:596-651`).

into the FCB (`src/cpm/bdosfn.asm:621-685`). A `?` in the FCB's name becomes

FCB naming the earlier extent gets 128 records and one naming a later, empty
extent gets 0. Open returns the entry's slot, 0 to 3, or `FFh` when no
matching extent exists (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:246-248`,

`ALLOCBLK` scans the vector from block 0 for the first clear bit, sets it
and puts the block's number in the FCB's map
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:683-774`). A delete clears the bits of each block the
entry lists (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:641-722`). The directory's own blocks are
set from `AL0` and `AL1` when the vector is built
(`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:503-532`), and they are never given out. The vector
changes as soon as a block is taken, before the file is closed. A block a
program has written but not yet closed is therefore already in use for every
other file. `ALLOCBLK` also marks the FCB as changed
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:733-763`). A close after a failed write can
still write the entry that holds the allocated block. Close can itself fail, so the entry is not guaranteed to reach the card
after a data-write error.
If the program exits without closing, the later vector rebuild derives
allocation from the directory again.

occurrences.full_context:
A vector is built when a drive is logged in, the first time it is selected
after a disk reset (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:202-350`). `LOGIN` calls the BIOS's
`SELDSK` for the drive's DPH, and a drive with no volume gets 0, which is
the `Select` error (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:212-222`). It copies from the DPH
the addresses of the translation table, the directory buffer, the DPB and
the vector. A volume the card marks read-only then goes into the read-only
vector (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:254-264`). For a drive not in `LOGINV`,
`INITALV` clears the vector and sets the directory's bits, and the drive's
bit in `LOGINV` is set. The whole directory is then read a record at a time.
`PARENT` sets the bit of every block that each entry in use lists and moves
the mark past the entry (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:268-350`,
`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:540-633`). A block number past the end of the volume
has no bit, and `BITPTR` passes over it (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:734-742`). The
drive still logs in, and a delete of that file passes over the number too.
For a drive already in `LOGINV`, `LOGIN` reads nothing: `LOGFAST` takes the
drive's mark from its DPH (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:362-385`).

- If the changed flag is set, the drive is taken out of `LOGINV` and put in
  `WARMV`, the vector of drives to rebuild to their mark
  (`src/ram.asm:260-261`). At its next selection `LOGIN` builds the vector
  again, but reads the directory only up to the mark
  (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:297-319`). The mark covers every entry recorded as
  used, so the scan can omit the remaining empty entries.
- If the flag is clear, `ALVSUM` adds up the vector's bytes with `SUMDE`,
  the routine that also sums the container's table
  (`src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:446-454`, `src/cpm/bdoslog.asm:473-496`,
  `src/volutil.asm:120-136`). If the sum is what `LOGDONE` stored, the drive
  stays logged in with its vector as it is. A different sum indicates a
  change that neither an allocation nor a directory write recorded, such as
  a stray write by a program. That drive is taken out of `LOGINV` and
  scanned in full at its next selection. Equal sums are not a byte-for-byte
  comparison of the vector.

occurrences.full_context:
The BDOS keeps its working state in RAM, from `BDOSRAM` up to the exclusive end
`BDOSRME`. In the retained `78127ec` map this is `BE76h–BEFFh`
(`78127ec:src/ram.asm:142-216`). The offered source defines the same block by
labels (`src/ram.asm:231-312`). Its 54-byte stack is at the top of that block
(`src/layout.asm:152`). Warm boot clears the block, as a fresh load of the BDOS
from disk would leave it, and sets the DMA address to `0080h`
(`src/boot.asm:530-539`). Two of the BDOS's variables are outside the block
because a warm boot must not clear them. `LOGINV`, in the BIOS's part of the
resident workspace, has a bit for each drive whose allocation vector the BDOS
has built (`src/ram.asm:62-65`). `PRGCODE`, the return code of function 108, is
above the RAM BIOS table, where only cold boot clears it (`src/ram.asm:386-388`,
`src/boot.asm:73-79`). Per-drive pointers and scan state are in the drive's DPH,
the 16-byte disk parameter header described in Chapter 17.

Each goes to `BDERR` with its message and code. What `BDERR` does is set by
the error mode, which function 45 puts in `ERRMODE`
(`src/cpm/bdos.asm:271-275`, `src/cpm/bdoscon.asm:47-72`). In the default
mode `DISKMSG` prints the message and `BDERR` waits for a key with `GETCHAR`
(`src/cpm/bdoscon.asm:108-137`). An ordinary key retained during message
output satisfies that wait. `^P` toggles list output and `^S` consumes a
resume key, with `^C` at that pause aborting
(`src/cpm/bdoscon.asm:318-350`). `CHDROP` then ends the program by warm boot, whatever the key, so the
function never returns to the program (`src/cpm/bdos.asm:115-119`). `CHDROP`
also drops the rest of a chained line, which Chapter 21 describes.

With `ERRMODE` at `FFh` the error returns to the program with `A` = `FFh`
and the error's code in `H`. Nothing is printed and the rest of a chained
line is kept. With `FEh` the message is printed first and the error returns
in the same way. Warm boot clears `ERRMODE` with the rest of the BDOS's
state, so each program starts in the default mode (`src/ram.asm:233-237`). A
read or write that returns an error leaves the FCB on the record it didn't
read or write, as CP/M 3's does (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:79-103`,

enter the BDOS through different state. The volume's read-only flag is in

(`src/cpm/bdosfn.asm:153-165`, `src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:35-41`,

new line. Built-ins can move `CMDSTRT` to an argument. CON moves it again
for a separated width, so its error may name that width. `ERRGO` sets

Both DIR and TYPE print through the pager. `PGINIT` takes `VHGT` and `VWID`,
or 24 rows and 80 columns for serial and reserves a row for `[more]`.
`PGPUT` resets its column at carriage return, steps back at backspace and
advances to the next multiple of eight at a tab. It counts
a new line at LF or before a printable character beyond the last column
(`src/cpm/ccpfile.asm:334-470`). At a pause function 6 reads a key without
echo. `UNMORE` erases the prompt with CR, six spaces and CR (`src/text.asm:32-33`).
The key mask
makes `#` equivalent to `^C` and `;` equivalent to Esc. `^C` and `#` drop
the chain. Esc, `Q`, `q` and `;` stop only the listing. Other keys continue
(`src/cpm/ccpfile.asm:475-520`). Chapter 21 explains the chain distinction.

SAVE erases an existing file, makes it again and writes two 128-byte records
per page from `0100h`. A failed make, write or close gives `NO SPACE`.
After a failed write it attempts close before reporting the error. A
successful close records the partial file. The error path discards the
close result, so the message does not certify that update. Digital Research's
CP/M 2.2 SAVE leaves the file open on that path
(`src/cpm/ccpcmd.asm:356-445`).

span ending at `WSEND`. That includes the retained command buffer, `CHPOS`
and `PRGCODE`, so a reset starts with no pending piece and a zero result

A program name occupies at least one character of its piece, leaving at
most 126 for the tail. `PREPPAGE` copies that tail to `0081h` and appends
a zero. At the maximum length, the zero lands at `00FFh`. One further
character would put it at `0100h`, over the program's first byte

byte at `0050h` lies below the tail and is written separately before entry
(`src/cpm/ccp.asm:498-525`, `src/layout.asm:72-79`).

`ERRGO` stores `RCFAIL`, or `FF00h`, before printing the error message.
`BADCMD` echoes the failed command or argument with a question mark and
falls through to that store (`src/cpm/ccp.asm:27-30`,
`src/cpm/ccp.asm:588-629`). `NO FILE` from `FILENO`, `FILE EXISTS` from
REN, `NO SPACE` from SAVE and COPY's four error messages all use `ERRGO`
(`src/cpm/ccpfile.asm:660-662`, `src/cpm/ccpmut.asm:181-184`,
`src/cpm/ccpcmd.asm:439-445`, `src/cpm/ccpmut.asm:379-381`,
`src/text.asm:34-41`). Missing programs, failed loads and unsuccessful
service installations reach `BADCMD` too. Startup's quiet absent-device
service path instead returns through `SVCOK` with the initial zero
(`src/cpm/ccp.asm:465-517`). Successful built-ins leave that zero.
COPY prints `COPIED` and its count, then sends the final newline through

(`src/cpm/ccpmut.asm:347-368`, `src/cpm/ccp.asm:619-629`).

(`src/cpm/bdos.asm:435-440`, `src/cpm/ccpcmd.asm:958-966`,

**21 Write sequential.** Writes the record at the DMA address at the FCB's
`CR` and moves on. It takes a new allocation block or a new extent when the
record falls in one (`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:22-207`). Returns 0 on success.
Returns 1 when the directory has no entry for a new extent or when the close
of the extent it leaves finds no entry for it. Returns 2 when the drive is
full. After a 1 the FCB stays on its extent with `CR` at 128, so a later
write, once an entry has been freed, makes the extent the FCB needs
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:119-175`). A block taken for a write that then fails
stays in the FCB's map. A later successful close publishes it in the entry
(`src/cpm/bdosrec.asm:733-767`). An FCB with the read-only attribute set gives
the `File R/O` error (`src/cpm/bdosfile.asm:430-445`).

The CPU generates the serial bits itself. It sends through `01h` bit 6 and
receives through `03h` bit 7. The connection uses 4800 baud, eight data bits,
no parity and two stop bits. The delay counts assume a 4 MHz clock, so the
board requires FAST with the 4 MHz oscillator (`tools/build.mjs:25-26`,
`tools/build.mjs:37-76`, `src/console.asm:387-421`,
`src/console.asm:452-492`).

heading_path.text: Appendix G. The TEC-1G as TEC-OS uses it
The hex keypad and its NMI

occurrences.full_context:
With the keypad NMI jumper fitted, a press raises a non-maskable interrupt. The
CPU pushes its return address and enters `0066h`, inside the default file
control block (FCB) at `005Ch–007Fh`. TEC-OS installs no NMI handler there. The
bytes can be file metadata rather than instructions, so a press can crash the
machine. The supported TEC-OS setup leaves the jumper off. The diagnostics ROM
has its own NMI test and different keypad instructions, which must not be
applied to an ordinary TEC-OS session.

address commands are `80h`, `C0h`, `94h` and `D4h`

heading_path.text: Appendix H. The service file format

occurrences.full_context:
A service file contains the bytes to install, the records it needs and the
positions that require relocation. Its on-disk header describes that work.
The loader overwrites some fields after using them, so an installed header
must be read differently from the file header below.
[Write a resident service](13-write-a-resident-service.md) covers authoring.
[Loading and removing services](24-loading-and-removing-services.md) follows
installation and gives the resident header. This reference retains a
historical GLCD.SVC dump to show the file fields and gap encoding together.

Blank lines are dropped. The new text uses CRLF line endings and a final

not itself cause an error when no rewrite is needed. Replacing STARTUP.CMD
can reuse its existing directory entries and blocks. A full directory causes

occurrences.full_context:
`?` matches one character, including a padding space. `*` fills the rest of
its field with question marks. Thus `G*.*` is `G???????.???`. Text after a
star in the same field is ignored, so `D*X` and `D*` select the same pattern.

TYPE takes one name without wildcards and no extra argument. It prints
through the pager until the first Ctrl-Z byte, `1Ah`, or the end of the

occurrences.full_context:
SAVE takes a decimal count from 0 to 255 and one unambiguous file name.
It writes that many 256-byte pages starting at `0100h`. A count of 0 makes
an empty file. The count must be less than the high byte of the word at
`0006h`, so the saved pages stop below the resident entry's page.
[Memory for programs](10-memory-for-programs.md) gives the memory boundary
and the complete capacity example.

occurrences.full_context:
For a program command the type is replaced by COM, except for SVC. Lookup
starts on the named drive, or the current drive when none is named, in the
current user area followed by user 0. The current user is restored after
that search. A file in user 0 needs no system attribute.

The reply goes through the selected console and is discarded in BAT mode.
Selecting an
unavailable console can leave or restore another mode, so the reply reports
the mode in effect, not merely the name typed. The practical alternatives
and recovery actions are in [Choose a console](06-choose-a-console.md).
